question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-3's definitions, how does BRRETA formally define a 'transaction broker'?
choice_a: A broker who exclusively handles the transfer of title at closing, with no other involvement
choice_b: Any broker who has completed more than 10 transactions in a calendar year
choice_c: A broker who represents only lenders, never buyers or sellers
choice_d: A broker performing only ministerial acts to assist a party, without forming a client/agency relationship with that party
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-3 defines a transaction broker as a broker who performs only ministerial acts to assist a party in a transaction, without establishing a client/agency relationship with that party -- a distinct, non-representative role recognized alongside single, dual, and designated agency.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-14, which of the following is an example of a 'ministerial act' a transaction broker may perform without creating a client relationship?
choice_a: Providing preprinted real estate form contracts, leases, and related exhibits and addenda
choice_b: Negotiating the purchase price on the party's behalf
choice_c: Advising the party on the maximum price they should offer
choice_d: Representing the party's interests as an advocate in the transaction
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-14(a) lists providing preprinted real estate form contracts, leases, and related exhibits/addenda -- along with identifying property, providing statistics, acting as a scribe, locating professionals, and identifying nearby facilities -- as ministerial acts a transaction broker may perform without becoming the party's agent.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-14(b), even though a transaction broker owes no fiduciary or agency duties, what obligations must the transaction broker still fulfill?
choice_a: None at all -- a transaction broker owes absolutely no duties of any kind to any party
choice_b: Timely presenting all offers, timely accounting for all money and property received, and timely disclosing known adverse material facts about the property's physical condition and about neighborhood conditions within one mile that are actually known to the broker
choice_c: A full common-law fiduciary duty identical to that of a single agent
choice_d: An obligation to personally guarantee the accuracy of a third-party home inspection
explanation: Even without forming an agency relationship, O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-14(b) requires a transaction broker to timely present offers, timely account for money and property received, and timely disclose known adverse material facts about the property's condition and about nearby (within one mile) neighborhood conditions that are actually known to the broker.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-14(c), when is a transaction broker held liable for information provided to a party?
choice_a: The broker is never shielded from liability, regardless of the source of the information or the broker's knowledge
choice_b: The broker is automatically liable for any inaccurate information regardless of source or knowledge
choice_c: The broker is liable only for the matters specifically enumerated in the section, and only upon a finding of fraud -- and is not liable for passing along inaccurate information if the broker disclosed its source and lacked actual knowledge it was false
choice_d: The broker is liable only if the party paid a separate consulting fee for the information
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-14(c) limits a transaction broker's liability to the matters enumerated in the section and requires a finding of fraud, and specifically shields the broker from liability for passing along information whose source was disclosed and which the broker did not actually know to be false.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-9, absent an earlier completion, expiration date, or authorized termination, how long does a BRRETA brokerage engagement (single agency, dual agency, or designated agency) generally continue by default?
choice_a: Indefinitely, with no default outer limit at all
choice_b: 90 days after the engagement began, regardless of any contrary agreement
choice_c: Until the licensee's next CE renewal cycle, regardless of when the engagement began
choice_d: One year after the engagement (or option) began, if no expiration date or termination occurs sooner
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-9 provides that a brokerage engagement continues until completed or, if earlier, until an agreed expiration date, an authorized termination, or -- absent either of those -- one year after the engagement (or option) began, whichever comes first.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-9(b), what duties does a broker continue to owe a former client after a brokerage engagement has terminated?
choice_a: Only accounting for all money and property from the engagement, and maintaining confidentiality of client information (unless the client permits disclosure, the law requires it, or the information has otherwise become public)
choice_b: The full range of statutory duties under Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8 continues indefinitely post-termination, unchanged
choice_c: No duties whatsoever survive termination of the engagement
choice_d: Only a duty to refer the former client to a new broker
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-9(b) narrows the broker's post-termination duties to just two: accounting for money and property from the engagement, and maintaining confidentiality of client information -- subject to exceptions for client permission, legal requirement, or information that has otherwise become public.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-9(c), if a broker's post-termination duty of confidentiality would conflict with the broker's separate duty to avoid providing false information to a customer, which duty controls?
choice_a: The confidentiality duty always prevails, even if it requires the broker to affirmatively mislead someone
choice_b: The duty against providing false information prevails and governs the broker's conduct
choice_c: Both duties are automatically waived whenever they conflict
choice_d: The broker must resign from the transaction entirely whenever any such conflict arises
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-9(c) resolves a conflict between the post-termination confidentiality duty and the duty to avoid providing false information by giving the anti-falsity duty priority -- a broker's confidentiality obligation does not permit affirmatively misleading someone.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-3's definitions section, how many separate defined terms does the section set out for BRRETA's brokerage-relationship framework?
choice_b: BRRETA contains no definitions section at all
choice_c: 14 definitional provisions, including terms such as agency, broker, client, designated agent, dual agent, and transaction broker
choice_d: 50 definitional provisions covering every term used anywhere in Title 10
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-3 sets out 14 definitional provisions establishing the vocabulary for BRRETA's brokerage-relationship framework, including agency, broker, client, designated agent, dual agent, and transaction broker, among others.

question: A buyer asks a licensee to simply show them a few listings and fill out a preprinted offer form, without wanting the licensee to negotiate or advise on price -- and no brokerage engagement agreement is signed. Under BRRETA, what relationship best describes the licensee's role here?
choice_a: Single agency, since any assistance to a buyer automatically creates a full agency relationship
choice_b: Designated agency, since the buyer is a distinct party from the seller
choice_c: Dual agency, since the licensee is assisting a party to the transaction
choice_d: Transaction broker performing ministerial acts, since no client/agency relationship was established and the licensee's involvement is limited to the kinds of ministerial acts enumerated in Section 10-6A-14(a)
explanation: Because no brokerage engagement was formed and the licensee's role is limited to enumerated ministerial acts (showing listings, providing forms) rather than negotiation or advocacy, this fits BRRETA's transaction-broker category under Sections 10-6A-3 and 10-6A-14, not single, dual, or designated agency.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-5, which sets out a broker's statutory duties when engaged by a seller, what must the broker do regarding offers received on the property?
choice_a: Present all offers and counteroffers to the seller in a timely manner, unless the seller has directed otherwise in writing
choice_b: Present offers only if they meet or exceed the seller's original asking price
choice_c: Present offers only after obtaining a second broker's independent review
choice_d: Withhold all offers below list price unless the buyer's agent specifically requests presentation
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-5 requires a broker engaged by a seller to timely present all offers and counteroffers to the seller, unless the seller has directed the broker in writing to do otherwise (such as a written instruction to stop presenting offers below a certain threshold).

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-5, what must a broker engaged by a seller disclose to the seller about adverse material facts?
choice_a: Nothing -- a seller's broker owes no disclosure duty to their own client regarding adverse facts
choice_b: Adverse material facts actually known to the broker pertaining to the physical condition of the property, and other adverse material facts actually known to the broker and not discoverable by the seller's own reasonably diligent inspection
choice_c: Only adverse facts about the buyer's creditworthiness, never facts about the property itself
choice_d: Adverse material facts only if the seller specifically asks the broker to investigate them
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-5 requires a seller's broker to disclose to the seller adverse material facts actually known to the broker about the physical condition of the property and certain other adverse material facts the broker knows and the seller could not reasonably discover.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-6, which sets out a broker's statutory duties when engaged by a buyer, what disclosure duty does the buyer's broker owe regarding the property's physical condition?
choice_a: The buyer's broker owes no disclosure duty of any kind, since the buyer is expected to conduct their own inspection
choice_b: Disclosing only facts that would increase the purchase price, never facts that could benefit the buyer
choice_c: Disclosing adverse material facts actually known to the broker pertaining to the physical condition of the property, similar in structure to the disclosure duty a seller's broker owes to the seller under Section 10-6A-5
choice_d: Disclosing adverse facts only if a licensed home inspector has already identified them in a written report
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-6 imposes a disclosure duty on a buyer's broker for adverse material facts actually known to the broker about the property's physical condition, structurally paralleling the seller-side disclosure duty under Section 10-6A-5, adapted to protect the buyer as the broker's client.

question: As a matter of general national agency doctrine (not itself a BRRETA-recognized brokerage-relationship category), what is 'subagency,' and how does it differ from the buyer/seller representation structures BRRETA affirmatively recognizes (single, dual, and designated agency)?
choice_a: Subagency and single agency are simply two different names for the exact same relationship
choice_b: Subagency requires the buyer to pay the seller's broker's entire commission directly
choice_c: Subagency is a relationship that can only exist between two salespersons, never between two brokers
choice_d: Subagency describes a cooperating broker who, through the MLS or another arrangement, acts as an agent of the listing broker (and thus of the seller) even while working with the buyer -- a structure largely supplanted in modern practice (including under BRRETA) by buyer agency, designated agency, and transaction-broker arrangements that more clearly define whom the cooperating licensee represents
explanation: Subagency -- historically, a cooperating broker acting as the listing broker's (and thus the seller's) subagent even while working with a buyer -- is a general national agency-law concept largely displaced in modern practice by clearer buyer-representation, designated-agency, and transaction-broker structures, including those BRRETA affirmatively recognizes in Georgia.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate agency-law doctrine (subagency), contrasted with BRRETA's recognized categories

question: If a Georgia licensee wants to purchase or sell property for their own personal account (rather than on behalf of a client), what does general national real estate ethics/agency doctrine expect regarding disclosure of the licensee's own status?
choice_a: The licensee must affirmatively disclose their status as a licensed real estate professional to the other party (or their representative) in the transaction, since a licensee's specialized market knowledge could otherwise create an unfair informational advantage if concealed
choice_b: No disclosure of the licensee's professional status is ever required in a personal transaction
choice_c: Disclosure is required only if the licensee is acting as a broker, never if acting merely as a salesperson
choice_d: Disclosure is required only for commercial property, never for the licensee's personal residence
explanation: As a matter of general national real estate ethics and agency-disclosure doctrine, a licensee buying or selling for their own account is generally expected to affirmatively disclose their licensed status to the other party, given the informational advantage a licensee's market expertise could otherwise create if left undisclosed.
source_note: hedge: standard national real estate ethics/agency-disclosure doctrine

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-4, is a broker's compliance with the specific statutory duties set out elsewhere in BRRETA (such as Sections 10-6A-5 through 10-6A-8) considered to satisfy the broker's reasonable-care standard?
choice_a: No -- compliance with the enumerated statutory duties has no bearing on whether the broker exercised reasonable care
choice_b: Yes -- a broker who complies with the specific duties enumerated in the applicable BRRETA section for that brokerage relationship is generally treated as having satisfied the statutory reasonable-care standard for that relationship
choice_c: Reasonable care is judged entirely independently of BRRETA and is instead governed exclusively by GREC administrative rule
choice_d: Only a court-appointed expert witness may determine whether a broker satisfied the reasonable-care standard, regardless of statutory compliance
explanation: Under BRRETA's structure, a broker's compliance with the specific statutory duties enumerated for the applicable brokerage relationship (e.g., the seller-duty list under Section 10-6A-5) is generally understood to satisfy the reasonable-care standard BRRETA substitutes for the common-law fiduciary standard.

question: Under general national brokerage-engagement practice (as reflected in agreements consistent with BRRETA's compensation-related provisions), when must a brokerage engagement agreement's compensation terms typically be disclosed to the client?
choice_a: Compensation terms need never be disclosed in writing under any circumstances
choice_b: Compensation may be disclosed verbally at closing for the first time, with no requirement it appear in the engagement agreement
choice_c: Compensation terms are typically addressed in the written brokerage engagement agreement itself, entered into at or before the broker begins performing brokerage services for that client
choice_d: Compensation terms must be filed with GREC before any brokerage engagement may begin
explanation: As a matter of standard brokerage-engagement practice consistent with BRRETA's framework, compensation terms are typically set out in the written brokerage engagement agreement the client signs at or before the broker begins performing services -- not left to a later, undocumented verbal disclosure.
source_note: hedge: standard national brokerage-engagement practice, consistent with BRRETA's written-engagement framework

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-7, which sets out a broker's statutory duties when engaged by a landlord, how does the general structure of these duties compare to the seller-duty structure in Section 10-6A-5?
choice_a: Section 10-6A-7 imposes no duties whatsoever on a landlord's broker
choice_b: Section 10-6A-7 applies only to commercial leases and has no application to residential leasing
choice_c: Section 10-6A-7 requires the landlord's broker to represent the tenant's interests equally alongside the landlord's
choice_d: Section 10-6A-7 parallels the Section 10-6A-5 seller-duty structure, adapted to a leasing context -- including timely presenting offers/applications to lease, timely accounting for money and property, and disclosing adverse material facts actually known to the broker about the property's physical condition
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-7 parallels the seller-duty framework of Section 10-6A-5, adapted for a landlord-engagement (leasing) context, including timely presentation of lease offers/applications, accounting for funds and property, and disclosure of known adverse material facts about the property's physical condition.

question: Under O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-8, which sets out a broker's statutory duties when engaged by a tenant, how does this duty structure compare to the buyer-duty structure in Section 10-6A-6?
choice_a: Section 10-6A-8 parallels the Section 10-6A-6 buyer-duty structure, adapted for a leasing context, including duties such as timely presenting lease offers on the tenant's behalf, accounting for funds and property, and disclosing adverse material facts known to the broker about the property's physical condition
choice_b: Section 10-6A-8 imposes no duties whatsoever on a tenant's broker
choice_c: Section 10-6A-8 requires the tenant's broker to represent the landlord's interests instead of the tenant's
choice_d: Section 10-6A-8 applies exclusively to tenants of commercial office space
explanation: O.C.G.A. Section 10-6A-8 parallels the buyer-duty structure of Section 10-6A-6, adapted for a tenant engagement, requiring the tenant's broker to timely present lease offers on the tenant's behalf, account for funds/property, and disclose known adverse material facts about the property's physical condition.
